claims.text: Conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2 requires sintering above 2300 °C.
Conventionally sintered ZrB2 typically retains residual porosity.
Residual porosity causes structural weakness in conventionally prepared ZrB2.
The proposed intervention is addition of approximately 2 wt% carbon to the ZrB2 precursor powder.
Carbon incorporation promotes grain-boundary diffusion during ZrB2 sintering.
Carbon-assisted grain-boundary diffusion enables ZrB2 densification at around 2000 °C rather than above 2300 °C.
Carbon incorporation reduces residual porosity in sintered ZrB2.
Residual porosity promotes pore coalescence and eventual failure during prolonged liquid plating-bath exposure.
Carbon atoms segregate to ZrB2 grain boundaries.
Carbon segregation at grain boundaries accelerates diffusion and promotes lower-temperature densification.
Greater densification produces a more uniform microstructure with fewer residual pores.
Fewer residual pores reduce sites for liquid infiltration and subsequent hole formation during plating-bath exposure.
ZrB2 containing approximately 2 wt% carbon and sintered at around 2000 °C will be denser and less porous than conventionally prepared ZrB2 sintered above 2300 °C.
The carbon-modified ceramic will form fewer or smaller holes and retain better structural integrity during prolonged liquid plating-bath exposure than conventionally prepared ZrB2.
The proposed benefit is expected near 2000 °C under an inert atmosphere.
The benefit may be less pronounced at higher sintering temperatures, in oxidizing atmospheres, or in exceptionally aggressive plating baths.
